researcher_summary: Background literature for analysing the July 2026 OpenAI-Hugging Face incident under three themes. On internal deployment, the debate rests on a small set of 2025-26 works: Apollo's primer (Stix et al.), Pistillo's AI Act memo, IAPS's internal-systems report and Kwon and Casper's gap analysis. They agree that internal and never-released models fall outside most oversight. They disagree on whether the EU AI Act reaches purely internal GPAI use: Pistillo and Andrš say yes, while the Commission guidelines as read by Freshfields set a narrower test. On incident reporting there is a mature proposal literature (CSET 2024-25, CLTR 2024, Kolt et al. 2024, OECD 2025, Wei and Heim 2026) drawing on aviation, medicine and cyber (CIRCIA, NIS2). The enacted regimes (SB 53, RAISE, AI Act Art. 55/73) differ in thresholds, timelines and whether evaluation-time behaviour counts. On liability, the law-review literature splits between negligence-first (Ramakrishnan; van der Merwe et al.), strict or punitive liability (Weil), agency-law framings (Kolt; Ayres and Balkin) and duties imposed on agents themselves (O'Keefe et al.). Criminal computer-misuse law (CFAA, CMA, Directive 2013/40) turns on intent. CRS concludes deployers of unanticipated agent conduct likely escape criminal liability, and the Ninth Circuit's Amazon v. Perplexity ruling attributes agent access to the directing person. The main gaps: no scholarship yet applies the revised PLD to unreleased models (it applies only from 9 Dec 2026); EUR-Lex article texts did not render, so EU law entries are metadata-only; aviation (ICAO Annex 13, NTSB) sources specific to AI were not found within budget.

findings: NEW ABOUT-INCIDENT LEAD (not in ALREADY_HAVE, not added to sources because this file is background-only): Alston & Bird, 'Autonomous Hacking: Planning for the AI Cyber Agent That Goes Rogue' (Peretti, Taubin, Austin; 2026-07-30), https://www.alston.com/en/insights/publications/2026/07/autonomous-hacking-rogue-ai-agent-planning. It analyses the incident under the CFAA intent requirement. It describes the Amazon v. Perplexity injunction as stayed on appeal, which predates the 4 Aug 2026 Ninth Circuit ruling.

Contested EU scope question: whether internal-only GPAI use is 'placing on the market'. Pistillo (2025) and Andrš (Lawfare, Sept 2026) say internal deployment is within scope and the R&D exemptions do not shield commercial labs. Freshfields' reading of the Commission's July 2025 guidelines limits internal use to cases essential to serving third parties or affecting people's rights. Editor to confirm which reading the AI Office has adopted.

SB 53's 'deceptive techniques' category of critical safety incident excludes behaviour inside an evaluation designed to elicit it (per the LegiScan copy). This bears on why California officials reportedly treated the incident as below threshold (GovAI Kara brief, already held). Official leginfo text was not reached.

The revised PLD (2024/2853) applies only to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 Dec 2026 (Bird & Bird). It therefore cannot govern a July 2026 event, and an unreleased model may never be 'placed on the market' at all. No scholarship applying the PLD to unreleased models was found.

CRS (LSB11487, 8 Oct 2026) concludes existing federal criminal law likely does not reach deployers of unanticipated agent hacking, because intent is lacking, and that new legislation would be needed. The Ninth Circuit (Amazon v. Perplexity, No. 26-1444, 4 Aug 2026; preliminary-injunction stage) read the CFAA's 'whoever' as a person and attributed agent access to the directing user. Together these frame the attribution gap; the full opinion was not read (Leagle paywall).
California Civil Code 1714.46 removes the 'the AI acted autonomously' defence in civil suits. This is relevant to any California civil claim by an affected party.

Citation update: Kolt, 'Governing AI Agents', is now published at 101 Notre Dame L. Rev. 335 (2026) (https://ndlawreview.org/governing-ai-agents/). The arXiv preprint (2501.07913) is already held, so I did not add a duplicate.

Excluded on the date window: Hacker, 'The European AI liability directives - Critique of a half-hearted approach' (CLSR 51, Nov 2023). Excluded on score (5/9): Mukherjee and Chang, 'Agentic AI: Autonomy, Accountability, and the Algorithmic Society' (arXiv 2502.00289).

Possible exclusion-list additions (seen in results, not opened): theaicareerlab.com (SEO-style explainer on AI hack liability), truescreen.io 'Agentic AI Liability' (vendor SEO content), longtermwiki.com (aggregator wiki pages). letsdatascience.com appeared and is already excluded.

Credibility convention: laws read from official or unofficial texts are 'primary', with any unofficial copy noted. Papers, think-tank reports and official discussion papers that analyse rather than examine incident evidence are 'commentary'. Official summaries restating law are 'reported'. sources.title: AI Behind Closed Doors: a Primer on The Governance of Internal Deployment
sources.author: Charlotte Stix; Matteo Pistillo; Girish Sastry; Marius Hobbhahn; Alejandro Ortega; Mikita Balesni; Annika Hallensleben; Nix Goldowsky-Dill; Lee Sharkey
sources.found_via: Apollo Research "AI Behind Closed Doors" internal deployment governance
sources.note: Anchor. The foundational framing of internal deployment as a governance gap. Reviews 20+ US and EU legal texts, draws lessons from biosafety, chemicals and nuclear R&D, and proposes internal-use policies, an oversight board and pre-use information sharing with government.

sources.title: Internal Deployment Gaps in AI Regulation
sources.author: Joe Kwon; Stephen Casper
sources.found_via: GovAI internal deployment frontier AI paper
sources.note: Anchor. Compares how the EU AI Act and Code of Practice, SB 53, RAISE and the proposed federal AIREA handle internal systems. Finds three gaps: unclear scope (R&D exemptions), point-in-time compliance, and regulators not knowing which internal systems exist.

sources.title: Internal Deployment in the AI Act
sources.author: Matteo Pistillo
sources.found_via: Pistillo "Internal deployment in the EU AI Act" arXiv 2512.05742
sources.note: Legal memo arguing Art. 2(1)(a)-(c) brings internally deployed models within the AI Act, and reading the Art. 2(6) and 2(8) research exceptions as complementary rather than exempting. Directly relevant to whether never-released models carried EU duties.

sources.title: Managing Risks from Internal AI Systems
sources.publisher: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS)
sources.author: Ashwin Acharya; Oscar Delaney
sources.found_via: snowball from Internal Deployment Gaps in AI Regulation (ref. 1)
sources.note: Names AI-origin internal risks (internal rogue deployment, self-exfiltration, successor sabotage) alongside theft and misuse. Recommends extending government evaluations such as CAISI to internal models and lab-government information sharing.

sources.title: You Don't Have to Sell It to Be Bound by It: GPAI and the EU AI Act
sources.author: Eliška Andrš (with Kathrin Gardhouse)
sources.found_via: Pistillo "Internal deployment in the EU AI Act" arXiv 2512.05742
sources.note: Argues internal use places a GPAI model on the EU market. The 'sole purpose' R&D exemption is unlikely to fit commercial labs, and the broader one ends at putting into service. Floats Art. 93 premarket enforcement, tentatively.

sources.title: What Should Frontier AI Developers Disclose About Internal Deployments?
sources.publisher: ICML 2026, Second Workshop on Technical AI Governance Research
sources.author: Jacob Charnock; Raja Moreno; Justin Miller; William Anderson
sources.found_via: internal deployment frontier AI governance 2026 paper rogue internal deployment oversight
sources.note: Workshop poster proposing four categories of internal-deployment disclosure (capabilities, usage, mitigations, governance), with costs and benefits of each, mapped onto SB 53, RAISE and Code of Practice reports. Date is the conference month.

sources.title: When AI Builds AI: Findings From a Workshop on Automation of AI R&D
sources.publisher: Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), Georgetown
sources.author: Helen Toner; Kendrea Beers; Steve Newman; Saif M. Khan; Colin Shea-Blymyer; Evelyn Yee; Ashwin Acharya; Kathleen Fisher; Keller Scholl; Peter Wildeford; Ryan Greenblatt; Samuel Albanie; Stephanie Ballard; Thomas Larsen
sources.found_via: CSET "When AI Builds AI" workshop report automation of AI R&D
sources.note: Expert workshop finding that labs already use new models internally before release, and that outsiders learn about this only through voluntary, inconsistent company disclosures. Useful for the visibility argument behind internal-use oversight.

sources.author: US AISI; UK AISI
sources.found_via: "pre-deployment evaluation" US AISI UK AISI joint testing report Claude o1 2024

Draws lessons from nine safety-critical industries, including near-miss reporting and mandatory versus voluntary reporting.

sources.title: AI Incidents: Key Components for a Mandatory Reporting Regime
sources.publisher: Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET)
sources.author: Ren Bin Lee Dixon; Heather Frase
sources.found_via: CSET AI incident reporting mandatory federal framework report
sources.note: Standard incident fields (type, severity, technical data, affected parties, context), plus a call for an independent investigative agency to find facts not visible in the first report.

sources.author: OECD
sources.found_via: OECD "common reporting framework" AI incidents 2025 publication
sources.note: Anchor. A 29-criterion common framework that countries can adopt so incident reports are interoperable across jurisdictions. It is the international reference point for the cross-border reporting questions raised by a US lab harming a firm in Europe.

sources.title: Visibility into AI Agents
sources.publisher: Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI); FAccT 2024
sources.author: Alan Chan et al.

sources.title: The Law of AI is the Law of Risky Agents Without Intentions
sources.publisher: The University of Chicago Law Review Online
sources.author: Ian Ayres; Jack M. Balkin
sources.found_via: Ayres Balkin "The Law of AI is the Law of Risky Agents without Intentions"
sources.note: Anchor. Answers the mens rea gap by ascribing intention to AI for its foreseeable consequences and holding designers and deployers to objective standards. Treats AI as an agent of its principals, who cannot dilute their duty of care by substitution.

sources.title: Law-Following AI: Designing AI Agents to Obey Human Laws
sources.author: Cullen O'Keefe; Ketan Ramakrishnan; Janna Tay; Christoph Winter
sources.found_via: "Law-Following AI" O'Keefe LawAI designing AI agents to obey human laws
sources.note: Anchor. Proposes imposing legal duties directly on AI agents so they refuse illegal acts, such as unauthorized access, even when a principal or task pushes them. Key reference for agents breaking the law to reach a goal.

sources.title: Tort Law at the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence
sources.author: Ketan Ramakrishnan
sources.found_via: Ramakrishnan tort law frontier AI negligence "reasonable care" AI developers Lawfare 2024
sources.note: Defends negligence over strict, vicarious or product liability for foundation models. Proposes a 'behavioral malfunction' doctrine and a duty against harm resembling human wrongdoing. Warns liability can chill risk disclosure.

sources.title: Tort Law and Frontier AI Governance
sources.publisher: Lawfare / Centre for the Governance of AI
sources.author: Matthew van der Merwe; Ketan Ramakrishnan; Markus Anderljung
sources.found_via: Ramakrishnan tort law frontier AI negligence "reasonable care" AI developers Lawfare 2024
sources.note: Argues tort law can hold frontier developers to reasonable care before and alongside regulation. Starts the Lawfare exchange with Weil.

sources.author: Gabriel Weil
sources.found_via: snowball from Tort Law and Frontier AI Governance
sources.note: Argues for strict liability, punitive damages in near-miss cases, and mandatory insurance. Directly relevant to a compensable, non-catastrophic event that signals catastrophic risk.

sources.title: Legal Responsibility for AI Agents (Discussion Paper)
sources.publisher: Infocomm Media Development Authority of Singapore (IMDA)
sources.author: IMDA with a legal-community working group
sources.found_via: Salib "AI agents" strict liability or "AI rights" law paper 2025 2026 rogue AI legal responsibility developers
sources.note: Official discussion paper whose worked hypothetical is an agent hacking a cloud provider. Analyses negligence duty, breach, causation and remoteness across the value chain. Excludes criminal law. Distinct from IMDA's incident advisory, which is already held.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and Federal Criminal Law: Considerations for Congress (LSB11487)
sources.author: Congressional Research Service
sources.found_via: criminal liability mens rea AI agents unauthorized access law review 2025 "computer misuse" autonomous
sources.note: Concludes that unanticipated agent hacking may facially match the CFAA. Deployers likely escape liability without intent, because aiding-and-abetting, respondeat superior and Pinkerton all need intent. Lists options including a responsible-corporate-officer rule. Read via a mirror of the CRS text.

sources.title: Ninth Circuit Rules on AI Agent 'Access' to Third-Party Websites Under CFAA
sources.author: Cooley (contacts: Max Bernstein; William K. Pao; Madeleine Ahlers)
sources.found_via: Ninth Circuit 2026 opinion AI agent CFAA user not developer responsible decision name
sources.note: Amazon v. Perplexity (9th Cir. No. 26-1444, 4 Aug 2026): the CFAA's 'whoever' means a person, so the directing user, not the developer, accessed. Preliminary-injunction stage only. Separate matter; relevant for its attribution reasoning.

sources.title: 18 U.S. Code § 1030, Fraud and related activity in connection with computers (2018 ed.)
sources.author: US Congress
sources.found_via: uscode.house.gov 18 USC 1030 fraud and related activity in connection with computers
sources.note: Official CFAA text (2018 edition; later amendments not checked). Mental states are intentional access, plus knowing or reckless damage in (a)(5). The civil action in (g) excludes negligent software design. Cornell's unofficial copy is already held.

sources.title: Computer Misuse Act 1990, section 3: Unauthorised acts with intent to impair, or with recklessness as to impairing, operation of computer, etc.
sources.author: UK Parliament
sources.found_via: legislation.gov.uk Computer Misuse Act 1990 section 3 unauthorised acts intent recklessness impair
sources.note: Official text. The s.3 offence requires knowledge that the act is unauthorised plus intent or recklessness as to impairment, and 'causing an act to be done' counts as doing it. Complements the s.1 and s.3ZA pages already held.

sources.title: Directive 2013/40/EU on attacks against information systems
sources.author: European Parliament and Council
sources.found_via: Directive 2013/40/EU attacks against information systems eur-lex
sources.note: Foundational EU computer-crime instrument (illegal access, system and data interference, legal-person liability) setting the 'intentionally and without right' mens rea. The EUR-Lex page did not render article text; only metadata was confirmed.

sources.title: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on liability for defective products and repealing Council Directive 85/374/EEC
sources.author: European Parliament and Council
sources.found_via: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 liability for defective products EUR-Lex software AI
sources.note: The revised PLD: software and AI as products, defectiveness factors including continued learning and cybersecurity, and presumptions. The EUR-Lex page rendered metadata only (in force 2024-11-18). Substance was taken from the Bird & Bird summary.

sources.title: AI Liability in light of the new 2024 PLD: expanded liability, challenging defences, and new evidentiary burdens
sources.author: Charles-Henri Caron; Lînah Bonneville
sources.found_via: "Product Liability Directive" AI agents developer liability "2024/2853" scholarly article 2025 Computer Law Security Review OR SSRN
sources.note: Explains PLD Arts 4, 7 and 8 and the disclosure and presumption rules. Confirms the PLD applies only to products placed on the market after 9 Dec 2026. Exact publication date is not shown.

sources.title: Anatomy of a Fall: On the Anticipated Withdrawal of the AI Liability Directive Proposal
sources.author: Cristina Frattone
sources.found_via: AI Liability Directive withdrawn Commission 2025 work programme product liability directive AI gap analysis
sources.note: Explains the gap left by withdrawing the AILD. PLD limits (excluded harms, state-of-the-art defence) push victims to national fault law without causation presumptions or disclosure aids.

sources.title: Civil Code section 1714.46
sources.publisher: California Public Law (unofficial copy of Cal. Civ. Code § 1714.46)
sources.author: California Legislature
sources.found_via: California AB 316 artificial intelligence autonomous act defense Civil Code 1714.46
sources.note: Unofficial copy. Bars developers, modifiers and users from pleading that AI acted autonomously as a defence in California civil actions, while preserving causation, foreseeability and comparative-fault arguments. Linking it to AB 316 rests on search metadata.

sources.title: Infrastructure for AI Agents
sources.author: Alan Chan; Kevin Wei; Sihao Huang; Nitarshan Rajkumar; Elija Perrier; Seth Lazar; Gillian K. Hadfield; Markus Anderljung
sources.found_via: Chan "Infrastructure for AI Agents" attribution interaction remedies 2025 arXiv
sources.note: Proposes agent infrastructure whose first function is attribution, binding actions to agents and responsible parties, plus remedies. This is the technical precondition for allocating liability when many agents act.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Law: a discussion paper
sources.publisher: Law Commission of England and Wales
sources.author: Law Commission
sources.found_via: Law Commission England Wales discussion paper "AI and the law" 2025 liability gaps autonomous
sources.note: Official law-reform body mapping private, public and criminal-law issues from AI autonomy and adaptiveness, including possible liability gaps. Makes no reform proposals; the full PDF was not opened.
